title: Net Profit Margin
subtitle: After everything - costs, interest, and tax - how much is left?
openingQuestion: What does Net Profit Margin = 5% mean?
openingOptions: For every 100 dong of revenue, 5 dong is net profit belonging to shareholders
The lowest margin in the industry
explanation: Net profit margin is what remains after everything - cost of goods, operating costs, interest, tax - so it is the one number that truly belongs to shareholders. Because it passes through so many layers, it is also easily distorted by one-off items: asset sales, tax refunds, revaluations. What counts as good depends on the industry: 5% is normal for retail and very low for pharma. And a thin margin can still produce a high ROE if asset turnover is fast enough.

diagram.label: What remains is Net Margin - the part that truly belongs to shareholders

realWorldExample.description: Airlines typically have Net Margins of only 3-8% due to heavy fuel, maintenance, and staffing costs, while software companies like Adobe can reach Net Margins above 25% - reflecting a fundamental difference in cost structure between the two industries.

quiz.question: What could cause Net Margin to fall while Operating Margin stays unchanged?
options: Rising interest expense or a higher tax rate - both sit below Operating Income
Rising COGS, letting cost of goods eat into profit before Operating Income is reached
Rising SG&A, making selling and admin costs higher during the period
Falling revenue, dragging both margins down at the same pace
quiz.explanation: Net Margin = Operating Margin − Interest/Revenue − Tax/Revenue. If Operating Margin is unchanged but Net Margin falls, the cause is rising interest expense or rising tax.

quiz.question: A company with only a 3% Net Margin but very fast Asset Turnover can still have an attractive ROE. What principle in financial analysis does this illustrate?
options: The company is certainly facing a serious profitability problem
ROE is the combined result of margin, turnover, and leverage
Asset turnover has no connection at all to a business's ROE
Net Margin is always the single most important metric, nothing else matters
quiz.explanation: This is exactly the insight of DuPont Analysis: ROE = Net Margin × Asset Turnover × Financial Leverage. A retailer with a thin margin but very fast sales can still post a solid ROE.

quiz.question: Net income is 90 billion, revenue is 1,800 billion. What is the Net Margin?
options: 9% (= 90 ÷ 1,000, revenue rounded down)
20x (= 1,800 ÷ 90, numerator and denominator swapped)
5% (= 90 ÷ 1,800, net income over revenue)
4.7% (= 90 ÷ 1,890, mistakenly adding profit into revenue)
quiz.explanation: Net Margin = Net Income / Revenue = 90/1,800 = 5%. After all costs, tax, and interest, every 100 dong of revenue keeps 5 dong for shareholders.

quiz.question: A business's Net Margin rises sharply while Operating Margin stays flat. What is the most likely cause?
options: Revenue is growing faster than all operating costs combined
The business has sharply cut its selling costs
Cost of goods sold fell thanks to cheaper raw materials
Interest expense or the tax rate has fallen during this period
quiz.explanation: The gap between these two margins is exactly interest and tax. If operations are unchanged but the bottom line improved, the improvement came from below the EBIT line - and that is often a one-off improvement, not a recurring one.

quiz.question: Why is a supermarket chain's 3% Net Margin less worrying than a software company's 3% Net Margin?
options: Because retail compensates with very fast asset turnover
Because supermarkets get more favorable tax treatment than software
Because software companies have much higher interest expense
Because retail recognizes revenue under a completely different method
quiz.explanation: DuPont multiplies margin by turnover: a supermarket turning its assets 2.5x a year still produces a good ROE on a 3% margin. Software turns over slowly and should have a much higher margin - a 3% margin there means something is broken.

keyTakeaways: After all costs, interest, and tax
Low margin + fast turnover can still produce a high ROE (the Walmart model)

practicePrompt.question: A company has Revenue = 1,000 billion, Operating Income (EBIT) = 150 billion; after subtracting 30 billion of interest and 24 billion of tax (20% on EBT), Net Income is 96 billion. What is this company's Net Margin?
options: Net Margin = EBIT / Revenue = 150/1,000 = 15%, since this is the most important profitability metric to track
Net Margin = 96/1,000 = 9.6% - meaning the company retains 9.6 dong of final net profit from every 100 dong of revenue, after subtracting every cost, interest, and tax
Net Margin cannot be calculated if you only know Net Income without knowing the company's Total Assets
Net Margin = Net Income / EBIT = 96/150 = 64%, since Net Income must be compared against EBIT rather than revenue
practicePrompt.explanation: Net Margin = Net Income / Revenue = 96/1,000 = 9.6%. This is the final (bottom-line) profitability metric, reflecting overall efficiency after subtracting every cost including capital structure (interest) and tax - unlike Gross Margin and Operating Margin, which only reflect production/operating efficiency.

summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: After all costs, interest, and tax

application.title: Calculate Net Margin
application.message: Divide Net Income by Revenue for a company you're following, then think about whether a low net margin comes with fast inventory turnover (the Walmart pattern).
application.secondary: A low net margin doesn't mean a bad company - it depends on the business model.

sections.text: Net Profit Margin is the final stop in the chain of margins: after subtracting everything, including interest and tax, what percentage of revenue does the business keep as real profit for shareholders?
What makes Net Margin different from Operating Margin

In essence: Net Margin = Operating Margin − (Interest Expense/Revenue) − (Tax/Revenue). If Operating Margin is unchanged but Net Margin keeps declining, the cause is almost certainly one of two things: the company took on more debt, raising interest expense, or the effective tax rate rose. That's why, when Net Margin is falling, the first thing to do is compare it against Operating Margin to isolate the cause, rather than rushing to conclude 'the core business is deteriorating.'
A low Net Margin doesn't mean a bad company

Airlines typically achieve only a 3-8% Net Margin due to enormous fuel, maintenance, and staffing costs, while a software company like Adobe can exceed 25%. But a company with only a 3% Net Margin and extremely fast asset turnover (the Walmart-style model) can still achieve an attractive ROE - this is exactly the insight of DuPont Analysis: ROE is the product of margin, asset turnover, and financial leverage, not margin alone.

items: Net Margin depends heavily on industry - always compare within the same industry
Net Margin falling but Operating Margin stable → suspect interest or tax, not the core business
Low margin + high turnover can still produce a good ROE - don't stop at a single metric
Net Margin is the final line - it bundles together every effect of capital structure and tax, making it hard to read operating efficiency 'cleanly' from it alone

lines: Net Margin tells you 'how much is left' - but to understand 'why it's left that way,' you need to unpack it through Gross Margin and Operating Margin first.
